doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Playing behind Getz versus Blakey; accompanying singers
summary: Blakey felt like jungle power, Getz demanded sensitivity and perfect pitch; she advises learning accompaniment from recordings and mentions Herbie behind Miles.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Right. How is it different playing behind him than with Blakey? Did you feel—

Well it was two totally different things. I mean with Art Blakey you felt like you had a jungle power every time you played. It was incredible. With Stan it was much more sensitive. You had to really listen to every note. It was like playing with a singer. You know, you had to play all the right notes, all the right voicings, play just the time he wanted to hear, and he never said that but you could tell from the way he was playing. And with Stan I just got so very spoiled because he played so in pitch, you know his pitch was so perfect it really bothered me a long time afterward to play with anyone who wasn’t aware of — they could play out of the pitch but if they didn’t know, if they couldn’t play around with it and know where that center was, and I’m the same way with singers, so I became that way then with horn players.
That’s an interesting statement about playing behind singers. What do you tell, do you have advice for piano players when they are going to have to branch out into that kind of accompaniment scene?

Well I think now you just go tell them to buy ten CD’s of your favorite singer and listen to the piano player. Because that’s the best way to actually hear what the possibilities are. It’s much easier than the way we had to learn hit and miss.

But you have to hear everything, you don’t want to put something just before — every little hair matters, everything matters. It has to be relaxed and swinging too. It’s a lot of balance is going on and you just need to know that plus the harmonies and the lines. There’s a lot to it.
Have you had occasion where you’ve tried experimenting with maybe some substitutions and so forth with different singers, and you find that — not to do it.

Well I don’t really play with singers but you know the first thing that I always tell, and not everyone does this so you don’t have to do this, you know the way Herbie was playing behind Miles. Sometimes it sounds, he’s just got his rhythmic thing, and it’s so much fun, seemingly having nothing to do with Miles you know. So you could play that way too. He was hooking up a lot with the rhythm section and I’m sure that’s what Miles wanted at that time, if we’re thinking back into the mid-60s. But I always, when I’m playing behind someone I just hear what notes they’re going to use and what notes they’re not going to use, and I’m certainly not going to play things that are going to offend that. I’ll stretch it as far as I can go but not — to make it sound like one thing.
